newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Chechen chief aims to meet Moslem leaders in Mecca.
newsitem.headline: Chechen chief aims to meet Moslem leaders in Mecca.

text.p: The secessionist president of Chechnya plans to make a pilgrimage this month to Mecca, where he hopes to hold diplomatic talks with leaders of Moslem states, Russia's RIA news agency reported on Sunday from the breakaway region.

Aslan Maskhadov, who was elected president of the North Caucasus region in January, told RIA he intended to "establish relations" with Moslem leaders also undertaking the annual haj pilgrimage to Islam's shrines in Saudi Arabia.

Maskhadov complained bitterly last week about a lack of progress in negotiations with Moscow on a lasting peace deal and economic compensation for the Chechens following the end of their 20-month war against Russian troops last year.

The president, who led his guerrilla forces to a dramatic victory last August, has been insisting on full sovereignty under international law for the mainly Moslem region of one million. The Kremlin refuses to countenance anything other than autonomy within the Russian Federation.
Moscow has warned other governments it will retaliate if any country establishes diplomatic relations with Chechnya.
Although the Chechens' war effort won sympathy and some discreet financial and practical support abroad, especially in the Moslem world, few nations are likely to risk Russia's wrath.
Saudi Arabia's King Fahd has ordered that 1,000 Chechens be invited to perform the pilgrimage to Mecca this month at his personal expense, Saudi newspapers said last week.
Maskhadov said he wanted to warn Moslem leaders against swindlers purporting to be soliciting funds on behalf of the Chechen authorities but actually financing illegal armed bands.

The mufti, or Islamic religious leader, of Chechnya was quoted as saying at the weekend that several planeloads of pilgrims had been authorised by Russian authorities to fly direct from their capital, Grozny, to Saudi Arabia this week.
Over 100 Chechen pilgrims in buses were reported to have been turned back by police at the border with the neighbouring Russian region of Dagestan on Friday due to passport problems.
Islam is flourishing across the former Soviet Union after seven decades of official communist oppression.

Maskhadov, who spent most of his life serving in the avowedly atheist Soviet army, has introduced moderate Islamic law to Chechnya. Most local people consider themselves Moslems but few have a thorough knowledge of the creed.
